source_refs.note: Exercise 9.2, Question 12 (book page 273); the book prints no answers for Exercise 9.2; answers checked with sympy and the solution book

blocks.explanation:
An identity between two inverse functions, true only on the given interval.
Plan: put \(\tan^{-1} x = \theta\), so the fraction inside \(\sin^{-1}\) becomes \(\sin 2\theta\).
Then check that \(2\theta\) lies in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), the principal range of \(\sin^{-1}\).
steps:
Given: \(-1 \le x \le 1\).
To prove: \(2\tan^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{1 + x^2}\).
Method: Let the inverse function be an angle (as in Example 8): \(\tan^{-1} x = \theta\). The fraction \(\frac{2x}{1 + x^2}\) is the double-angle form \(\frac{2\tan\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta} = \sin 2\theta\), so the right side becomes \(\sin^{-1}(\sin 2\theta)\).

Let the inverse be an angle
\[\tan^{-1} x = \theta\]
\[x = \tan\theta\]
Why: Definition of \(\tan^{-1}\); the angle \(\theta\) lies in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

Use the interval \(-1 \le x \le 1\)
\[-1 \le \tan\theta \le 1\]
\[-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \le \theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{4}\]
\[-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le 2\theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
Why: \(\tan\) is increasing on \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and \(\tan\left(\pm\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \pm 1\). Doubling keeps the inequalities.

Rewrite the fraction
\[\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2} = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta}\]
\[= \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{\sec^2\theta}\]
\[= 2\,\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\,\cos^2\theta\]
\[= 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta\]
Why: \(1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta\); dividing by \(\sec^2\theta\) is multiplying by \(\cos^2\theta\); and \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta\).

Take \(\sin^{-1}\)
\[\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2}\]
\[= \sin^{-1}(\sin 2\theta)\]
\[= 2\theta = 2\tan^{-1} x\]
Why: \(\sin^{-1}(\sin u) = u\) only when \(u\) lies in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\); step 3 showed that \(2\theta\) does. This is exactly why the question gives \(-1 \le x \le 1\).

Check
\[x = 1:\ 2\tan^{-1} 1 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
\[\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2}{2} = \sin^{-1} 1 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
\[x = \tfrac{1}{2}:\ 2\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{2} \approx 0.9273\]
\[\sin^{-1}\tfrac{4}{5} \approx 0.9273\]
Why: Both sides agree. Outside the interval the result fails: at \(x = \sqrt{3}\), \(2\tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\) but \(\sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}\).
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(2\tan^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{1 + x^2}\) for \(-1 \le x \le 1\).
